# DevOps Interview Preparation Academy: Learning Content

Stage 2 only. No website, deployment, learner scores, or professional experience is created by these files. Authority: [Stage 1 audit](../academy-resume-audit.md). Original resume, roadmap and progress files remain unchanged.

Start with [the schedule](content/roadmap/README.md), then its linked daily lesson. Machine-readable navigation and coverage live in [plan.json](content/roadmap/plan.json). All paths in lab commands are relative to this `academy-content` directory unless a lesson explicitly says Ubuntu VM.

## The 90-minute contract

20 minutes concepts, 40 minutes **one** guided/independent/challenge lab, 20 minutes investigation and interview, 10 minutes revision. The three levels are alternatives, not extra compulsory homework. Projects reuse the daily artifacts across several sessions. Installation, downloading images and debugging setup consume lab time. Stop at 90 minutes and carry work forward. Thirty sessions total 45 hours; this is not a promise of mastery or employment readiness.

## Attempt-first practice

Guided examples are available to study. Independent tasks give requirements and success criteria, not solutions. Record your attempt, observed output and hypothesis first. Then open the relevant hint in [the hint book](content/troubleshooting/hints.md). Only after retrying consult [the solution book](content/troubleshooting/solutions.md). Answers are separate files, not securely locked: Markdown cannot enforce an attempt gate. The future website must enforce the presentation gate without pretending it can hide bundled source from an inspector.

The interview bank is also split into [questions](content/interview-questions/questions.json) and [answer references](content/interview-questions/answers.md). Say your answer before opening the reference. Assess correctness /3, practical understanding /2, evidence /2, clarity /2, coverage /1; record first and assisted attempts separately. Self-scoring is not expert or AI grading.

## Lab safety and prerequisites

- Nothing here authorizes company or production access. All supplied evidence is synthetic **training simulation**, and all configurations are **personal lab examples**, not employer architecture.
- Use a dedicated Ubuntu 24.04 VM for systemd/Linux. Do not execute VM installation, permission or service commands on macOS. A normal Docker container is not a systemd VM. A VM installer and its hypervisor are prerequisites to choose locally; no unattended privileged installer is provided.
- Host labs need Git, Python 3.11+, curl, OpenSSL, Docker Desktop, kubectl, kind, Helm 3+, and Terraform 1.10+ as used. Use official installers. macOS `ps`, `free`, `ss`, `systemctl`, `timeout` and GNU flags differ; Linux commands are labeled. Check versions before starting. Docker/VM memory consumption is a real local cost.
- Ruby 2.6+ is used for dossier inspection and the content validator; ensure it exists in whichever environment runs those commands. The alternative Java lab needs JDK 17 and Maven 3.9 or compatible Gradle 8.14. Optional telemetry needs a verified Python 3.11/3.12 SDK environment, not an assumption that all new Python versions are supported.
- Use a writable copy of lab configurations in your own training directory for independent edits. Do not edit the original resume, original roadmap, shared source, or any work repository. Private evidence and generated plans/state belong outside Git.
- Local application listeners default to loopback. A container binds internally to `0.0.0.0` only when explicitly configured; Docker publishes to `127.0.0.1`. Never expose the training fault endpoints publicly.
- The named local cluster is `academy`; its explicit context is `kind-academy`. Core Kubernetes mutations use that context. Confirm `kubectl --context kind-academy cluster-info` matches your local Docker-created cluster. The optional approved EKS extension instead requires an explicitly verified sandbox context and endpoint. A namespace alone is not a safety boundary.
- Run only one HTTP listener per listed port. Stop foreground lab servers with Ctrl+C in their own terminal. Do not kill unrelated processes or delete unnamed resources to free a port.
- Optional AWS work requires an approved sandbox, explicit account/profile/region, a cost budget, owner and cleanup plan. EKS control plane, EC2 nodes, EBS, ALB, NAT, ECR storage, S3, Secrets Manager, telemetry and transfer can incur costs. Budget alerts are not spending caps. No cloud provisioning is required for the daily core plan.
- Before any approved AWS read, set `export AWS_PAGER=""` and inspect `aws sts get-caller-identity --profile "$LAB_PROFILE"`. Do not print tokens, secret values, kubeconfig or Terraform state. Logs, plans, rendered charts and environment dumps may also contain secrets.
- Identity, telemetry and paid scanning exercises default to supplied evidence. No Entra tenant, Datadog, Rollbar, Snyk or AWS access is assumed. Never paste credentials into Markdown, Git, an answer, or a terminal command recorded by the assistant.
- Tags in examples are explicit but not immutable. For a real approved deployment resolve and review image digests, tool versions and action commit SHAs against current official releases. A lab fixture is not a hardened production baseline.

## Content conventions

Daily lessons use ten fixed sections and explicit resume IDs. Concepts also state purpose/problem/terms; architecture states workflow; examples, integrations, mistakes and interview framing are included. Each major area includes guided, independent and challenge practice. Daily `plan.json` rows point to questions and incident IDs, and map the audit's R01-R56 and C01-C24 identifiers. S01-S10 are prerequisites, not additional employment claims.

Examples of expected output are illustrative. IDs, PIDs, addresses and timings vary. A fixture replay is not a real cloud test. [VALIDATION.md](VALIDATION.md) distinguishes checks actually performed from unexecuted infrastructure labs.

## Course navigation

- [Roadmap](content/roadmap/README.md)
- [Five practical projects](content/projects/README.md)
- [Incident dossiers](content/troubleshooting/incidents.json)
- [Resume defense and engineering evidence](content/resume-defense/defense.md)
- [Supplementary tool deep-dives](content/reference/secondary-tools.md)
- [Validation and limitations](VALIDATION.md)

No progress is pre-populated. Employment/contribution clarification remains pending. Completing a lab supports the statement "I practised this in a lab," not "I operated it in production."

# Validation and limitations

This report concerns authored content and fixtures, **not learner progress**. No company or production system was used. No website, server deployment, hosted workflow, AWS resource or SaaS account was created. Original resume/roadmap are protected by recorded SHA-256 checks in the validator.

## Repeatable content checks

From the academy-content root, run `ruby tools/validate.rb`. Ruby uses standard libraries only. It checks ordered days, timing, audit coverage, daily sections, question/answer mappings, incident/help counts, Markdown links/fences, Bash syntax without execution, JSON/plain YAML/Maven XML, original fingerprints and common accidental state/key artifacts. Helm templates require Helm rendering separately. Syntax checks do not establish remote API compatibility, access permissions or safe runtime outcomes. The accidental-file check is not a comprehensive secret scanner.

The full content check passed on 2026-10-30: 30 lessons, R01-R56, C01-C24, S01-S10, 100 question/answer pairs, 40 incident/hint/solution sets, five projects, 44 Markdown files with valid local links, 53 Bash/sh fenced blocks and 12 plain YAML files. All JSON and Maven XML parsed. The original PDF and roadmap fingerprints matched. Editor diagnostics reported no errors in academy-content. These results validate structure and syntax, not the operational integrations listed below.

## Focused checks already performed

- Python standard-library sample: three unit/in-process HTTP tests passed; the ephemeral listener used loopback and shut down. Pylance syntax checks passed for the app and test file.
- Bash health script syntax passed; this alone is not a full network integration test.
- Terraform formatting and init/validate passed in a fresh temporary copy with backend disabled, using only the built-in terraform_data resource. No cloud provider, apply, import or state migration was executed.
- Helm lint and QA render passed. A string replica count was rejected by the schema; HPA rendering omitted the Deployment replica field to avoid ownership conflict. No cluster install/upgrade was executed.
- Intermediate structure checks passed for 30 lessons, 100 question/answer pairs, 40 incidents and five projects. Final cross-file checks remain separately identified.

## Not executed and prerequisites

Docker builds/containers, kind creation, Kubernetes manifests, HPA/metrics-server, Nginx runtime, systemd installation and ArgoCD installation/sync were **not run by the authoring assistant**. kind was not installed in the inspected host. Docker CLI availability does not prove a running daemon; kubectl availability does not authorize any context. The Ubuntu VM and appropriate memory/disk capacity remain learner prerequisites.

Java/Maven/Gradle builds, optional ddtrace/Rollbar SDK behavior, Snyk scanning, hosted GitHub triggers/callers/OIDC, ECR push, S3 backend locking, real EKS/ALB networking and Datadog/Rollbar ingestion were not executed. Java source/build metadata and optional dependency ranges are teaching fixtures, not a current security/support certification. Optional telemetry should use a verified compatible Python 3.11/3.12 environment; the inspected terminal had Python 3.15. Never equate parsing with these integrations passing.

No live URL checks guarantee future availability of external installers/releases. Review official versions, compatibility and supply-chain integrity before optional setup. Packages/images may need internet and local disk; initial setup may consume a whole session.

## Approvals and missing information

- Clarify actual employment dates, role and personal contributions before rehearsing professional claims. No numerical achievement or historical incident has been invented.
- Authorized personal repository and permission for hosted Actions/push are needed for live workflow exercises. Example workflows remain outside .github/workflows and cannot auto-run here.
- Real cloud labs require an explicit sandbox account/profile/region, owner, budget, least-privilege permissions, private connectivity and cleanup plan. Budget alerts do not cap spend. The course never modifies company Terraform state, production clusters or tenant roles.
- Datadog/Rollbar/Snyk/Entra execution requires approved test access, private credential handling and data/cost review. Local spans/test events do not prove full application instrumentation or distributed tracing.
- Markdown separates attempts, hints and solutions but cannot enforce access gates. A future website can gate presentation; no static client can securely hide answers bundled with it.

## Scope and preservation

All Stage 2 additions are under academy-content. The original PDF, roadmap, progress record and Stage 1 audit have not been edited. No scores, completed days or assessed weaknesses are pre-populated. The five projects compose the daily work; optional extensions replace a lab block or carry forward, rather than silently extending 90 minutes.

# Day 21: ArgoCD and reconciliation

Resume: R15/R27/R30/R33; C12. Time: 20/40/20/10. Local optional installation; otherwise Application/render evidence. Repository access must be authorized.

## 1. Learning objectives
Explain source, destination, reconciliation, sync and health. Distinguish application operation from administering ArgoCD itself.

## 2. Concepts
GitOps keeps desired state in Git and reconciles it through a controller. ArgoCD's API/server handles user interaction, repository components retrieve/render sources, and the application controller compares/reconciles cluster state. An Application selects repoURL, targetRevision, path and destination. Sync means agreement with desired manifests; health is resource/application readiness assessment, not an end-to-end availability guarantee.

## 3. How it works
Read source revision -> render chart -> compare live objects -> display differences -> authorized sync -> observe resource health. The example uses manual sync and a local destination, with namespace creation enabled. No automated pruning/self-healing is silently enabled. Helm templating under ArgoCD does not necessarily create a Helm release with ordinary Helm history.

## 4. Real-world usage
The resume claims monitoring sync and health and diagnosing failures. Repository credentials, incorrect paths and destination RBAC fail at different stages. Do not infer the real platform's automatic sync policy from the word GitOps.

## 5. Hands-on lab
Core, no controller required:
```bash
helm template gitops fixtures/helm/academy --namespace academy-gitops
ruby -rjson -e 'puts JSON.pretty_generate(JSON.parse(File.read("content/troubleshooting/incidents.json")).find { |item| item["id"] == "I21" })'
```
Read `fixtures/argocd/application.yaml` and resolve every field. The REPLACE repository must not be applied. For the optional live local path use Project 4's version-reviewed installation and authorized Git repository instructions. Once its prerequisites are fulfilled, inspect with `kubectl --context kind-academy -n argocd get application academy -o yaml`; avoid copying credentials or repository Secrets. Setup consumes the lab block and can carry over. Cleanup: preserve the lab controller for day 22, then use Project 4's cleanup.

## 6. Expected output
Rendered GitOps-named Service/Deployment and a mapped Application contract. Live mode should display source comparison and health; if no controller is installed, an Application CRD error is expected and must not be described as a completed GitOps deployment.

## 7. Troubleshooting
I21: check repo reachability/auth, target revision/path and Helm rendering before destination access. ComparisonError differs from a successful sync with unhealthy Pods. Fix source/config at its owning layer, refresh comparison and verify workload behavior. Do not widen destination RBAC to cluster-admin without a justified lab-only requirement.

## 8. Interview preparation
Q41/Q42: Synced versus Healthy and Git as desired-state source. Explain the controller's responsibilities without placing it in the runtime HTTP request path.

## 9. Independent practice
Write an Application for a fictional approved repository and explain the consequences of changing path, revision and namespace. Do not push or register that repo during content work. Challenge I21 -> H21 -> S21.

## 10. Revision
Repo/render/destination/app failures are different. Record whether your evidence came from local rendering, fixtures or an actual authorized local controller. Revisit Terraform partial failure reasoning.

# Day 22: GitOps promotion and recovery

Resume: R01/R27-R33/R53; C09/C12/C22. Time: 20/40/20/10. Reuse Project 4 or solve synthetic evidence; no new platform setup today.

## 1. Learning objectives
Track source commit, image digest and deployment-config commit separately. Recover desired state without fighting reconciliation.

## 2. Concepts
OutOfSync means desired/live comparison differs; it is not automatically an outage. Self-healing can undo live edits. Pruning can delete tracked resources absent from desired state; reviewing deletion scope is essential. Promotion should reuse a verified artifact with an explicit environment configuration change. A Git revert records a new change; resetting history is not the normal audited recovery path.

## 3. How it works
CI publishes immutable image -> reviewed config commit changes chart/image reference -> ArgoCD observes revision -> reconciles -> probes/telemetry establish recovery. If a desired configuration is bad, revert/correct it through review; a live-only rollback may be overwritten. Emergency manual action needs coordination and reconciliation of Git afterward.

## 4. Real-world usage
This connects the resume's pipelines, Helm values and per-environment ArgoCD applications. Deployment flow and runtime request flow are separate. A green sync cannot establish low error rate; a pushed image alone cannot establish deployment.

## 5. Hands-on lab
For a configured local Application:
```bash
kubectl --context kind-academy -n argocd get application academy -o jsonpath='{.status.sync.status}{" "}{.status.health.status}{"\n"}'
kubectl --context kind-academy -n academy-gitops get deployments,pods,services
git diff -- fixtures/helm/academy
git log -3 --oneline
```
Git commands apply only inside your separate authorized lab repository; do not run them against employer content. Review one proposed image-version/values change and its rendered diff before any push/sync. If no live repo/controller is available, I22 supplies desired/live/history evidence and the same decision task. Cleanup: return the local lab to a known-good desired configuration, then stop forwards; retain for Project 4 verification.

## 6. Expected output
In live mode actual statuses and Pod health; in fixture mode a documented mismatch and recovery proposal. `Synced Healthy` is only part of success: call the Service and inspect version/error evidence before declaring recovery.

## 7. Troubleshooting
I22: establish source revision and live change -> inspect diff -> identify owning controller -> choose Git correction or coordinated emergency action -> sync -> verify endpoints/telemetry. For unexpected pruning, stop automated destructive operations and inspect affected scope before approving anything. Do not blindly enable prune as an OutOfSync fix.

## 8. Interview preparation
Q43/Q44: explain why a manual change disappears and how to roll back a GitOps release. State any downtime/data-compatibility limitations rather than claiming instant universal rollback.

## 9. Independent practice
Draw a promotion from dev to QA using the same digest and separate config approvals. Write a recovery plan for a wrong image tag. Challenge I22 -> H22 -> S22 after evidence review.

## 10. Revision
Reconcile the source of truth; do not fight it. Distinguish image, chart, source and config versions. Revisit Helm's rendered values versus cluster state.

# Day 5: VPC, ALB and environment boundaries

Resume: R01-R03/R07/R08/R53; claims C03/C06/C22. Time: 20/40/20/10. Core lab is synthetic data analysis, free and local. No AWS credentials needed.

## 1. Learning objectives
Trace a request and its return path across network and identity boundaries. Explain five environments as a resume claim requiring evidence, not five environments you must provision for practice.

## 2. Concepts
A VPC is a logically isolated network; subnets occupy availability zones. Route tables select a next hop. An internet gateway enables eligible public connectivity; a NAT gateway commonly enables private IPv4 outbound access, not unsolicited inbound traffic. Security groups are stateful allow rules; NACLs are stateless allow/deny rules that need return-path reasoning. Separate accounts improve isolation but add management cost.

## 3. How it works
Client resolves Route 53 alias -> connects to ALB listener -> rule selects target group -> healthy target receives request -> response returns. Routes, addresses, SGs and NACLs must agree. ALB IP targets reach Pod IPs; instance targets use node/NodePort routing. EC2 worker nodes are supporting EKS knowledge, not an explicit standalone service claim. A public subnet route does not itself assign a public IP.

## 4. Real-world usage
This is the foundation of the resume's networking/DNS and multi-account responsibilities. Architecture diagrams must distinguish environment, account, cluster and namespace; two namespaces do not simulate five-account isolation. Secrets and Terraform state need their own environment boundaries too.

## 5. Hands-on lab
Read incident I05 from the dossier with this local JSON inspection command:
```bash
ruby -rjson -e 'items=JSON.parse(File.read("content/troubleshooting/incidents.json")); puts JSON.pretty_generate(items.find { |item| item["id"] == "I05" })'
```
This prints synthetic observations only, not the solution. Draw subnet routes, ALB/target ports and return traffic; label the identity that configures resources separately from packet filtering. Select one evidence card, record what it rules out, then request the next. Allocate 10 minutes to the drawing, 20 to diagnosis, 10 to verification/prevention design. Cleanup: none; save your drawing privately.

## 6. Expected output
The fixture describes a successful DNS/TCP-to-ALB path and an unhealthy backend. Your output is a diagram plus a justified failed boundary, not a guessed AWS CLI response. Record whether the problem is routing, security filtering, application listener or health path; more than one can coexist.

## 7. Troubleshooting
Use symptom -> possible causes -> target health reason -> listener/port -> route/SG/NACL -> narrowed cause -> scoped proposal -> repeated health and request checks -> prevention. In an approved sandbox only, `aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn "$LAB_TARGET_GROUP_ARN" --profile "$LAB_PROFILE" --region "$LAB_REGION"` reads health metadata. Set AWS_PAGER and verify caller identity first. Never fix this by opening all inbound traffic.

## 8. Interview preparation
Q09/Q10: explain route versus permission, stateful versus stateless, and account versus namespace isolation. Discuss availability and costs rather than asserting five clusters are always the best design.

## 9. Independent practice
Draw one alternative that keeps workloads private but serves public HTTPS. Explain management access separately. Challenge I05 -> H05 -> retry -> S05. No resource creation is required or authorized.

## 10. Revision
Reachability needs every layer, and return traffic matters. DNS is not a request proxy. ALB, NAT, EC2 and EKS cost money when provisioned. Revisit day 2: identity/configuration differs from network connectivity.

# Day 7: IAM, access and secret boundaries

Resume: R01/R03/R10/R17/R42; claim C05. Time: 20/40/20/10. Synthetic policy review; no account or fee required.

## 1. Learning objectives
Separate authentication, role trust, action permissions and secret delivery. Explain the effective permission decision rather than looking for any one Allow statement.

## 2. Concepts
A principal is an acting identity. A role is assumable identity with permissions; its trust policy controls who may assume it. Identity policies permit actions on resources; resource policies and additional boundaries may also matter. An explicit deny overrides applicable allows. A secret is sensitive data, not a permission grant. Kubernetes Secret base64 encoding is not encryption.

## 3. How it works
Caller authenticates -> may assume a trusted role -> request action/resource/context is evaluated -> service allows or denies -> application handles the result. STS temporary credentials expire. Secrets Manager retrieval separately depends on identity, network/service reachability and possibly KMS authorization; rotating a value does not guarantee an already-running process reloads it.

## 4. Real-world usage
The resume claims least-privilege AWS access and supported OIDC. EKS administrator access, Pod AWS identity and a CI role are different identities. Do not give a workload a node's broad role to solve one denied action. Entra/product RBAC is a different authorization system, revisited on day 27.

## 5. Hands-on lab
Read the supplied narrow publishing policy and incident:
```bash
python3 -m json.tool fixtures/aws/ecr-publish-policy.json
ruby -rjson -e 'puts JSON.pretty_generate(JSON.parse(File.read("content/troubleshooting/incidents.json")).find { |item| item["id"] == "I07" })'
```
The JSON command validates/formats a **dummy** policy, not AWS authorization. For each statement write principal, action, resource and relevant conditions. Explain why ECR token retrieval uses resource `*`, while repository actions are scoped. Identify the placeholder account/region and do not install this policy. Draw the separate dummy Secret and Secrets Manager retrieval paths. Cleanup: none.

## 6. Expected output
Two readable policy statements and synthetic evidence. Your result is an action/resource matrix and a reasoned denial, not an IAM simulator verdict. A syntactically valid policy can still be wrong or dangerously broad.

## 7. Troubleshooting
I07: verify actual principal before checking trust or permissions; compare exact API action/resource, policy conditions and explicit denies. In an approved sandbox, `aws sts get-caller-identity --profile "$LAB_PROFILE"` is an identity check, not proof of permission to other services. Also consider organization policies, boundaries and endpoint policies when applicable. Safe fix: minimum approved permission change, then test both permitted and forbidden behavior.

## 8. Interview preparation
Q13/Q14: role versus policy, trust versus permissions, and secrets versus authorization. Explain why OIDC is not "no credentials": it replaces long-lived keys with short-lived credentials.

## 9. Independent practice
Design permissions for a CI job that can publish to one repository but not delete repositories. List the denied operations and test strategy. Challenge I07 -> H07 -> retry -> S07. Do not widen a real policy.

## 10. Revision
Identify actor, action, resource and conditions. Base64 is reversible. Never print real Secret values, Terraform state or environment dumps. Revisit network layering before blaming IAM for a timeout.

# Day 12: S3, ECR, Secrets Manager and CloudWatch

Resume: R05/R06/R09/R10; C04/C05/C14. Time: 20/40/20/10. Local fixture analysis; optional AWS reads require an approved sandbox.

## 1. Learning objectives
Explain each service's responsibility and fully investigate one access failure. Do not attempt four separate cloud implementations in 40 minutes.

## 2. Concepts
S3 stores objects identified by keys; versioning can help recover overwritten objects but is not a complete recovery process. ECR stores container manifests/layers; tags are names and digests identify content. Secrets Manager manages secret versions and rotation workflows. CloudWatch collects AWS metrics/logs and evaluates alarms by dimensions, period and threshold. Each service evaluates identity and may incur storage/API/ingestion costs.

## 3. How it works
Caller identity -> service endpoint -> authorization/context -> operation -> response. S3 state access is not the same as owning the infrastructure represented by state. A secret can rotate while an application keeps an old cached value. An alarm needs a matching metric stream, correct evaluation and a configured notification path.

## 4. Real-world usage
These services explicitly support the resume's delivery, configuration and monitoring. Terraform state in S3 can contain secrets even when outputs are marked sensitive. Datadog and CloudWatch can complement one another without assuming identical collection paths.

## 5. Hands-on lab
Analyze I12 and create four rows: stored data, caller, verification and likely failure:
```bash
ruby -rjson -e 'puts JSON.pretty_generate(JSON.parse(File.read("content/troubleshooting/incidents.json")).find { |item| item["id"] == "I12" })'
python3 -m json.tool fixtures/aws/ecr-publish-policy.json
```
Choose one S3 or ECR denial and explain which identity/action/resource to check. Optional metadata-only examples, after setting verified LAB_PROFILE/LAB_REGION/LAB_BUCKET/LAB_SECRET_ID in your own approved shell:
```bash
export AWS_PAGER=""
aws sts get-caller-identity --profile "$LAB_PROFILE"
aws s3api get-bucket-versioning --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" --profile "$LAB_PROFILE" --region "$LAB_REGION"
aws secretsmanager describe-secret --secret-id "$LAB_SECRET_ID" --profile "$LAB_PROFILE" --region "$LAB_REGION"
```
These read metadata, not secret values; redact identifiers before sharing. Skip them without authorization. Cleanup: no resources created; retain only sanitized local reasoning.

## 6. Expected output
Core output is a four-service boundary map and one justified denial. Approved S3 metadata may show Enabled or no versioning status; neither is universal. DescribeSecret should not return the secret payload. Do not invent successful AWS results.

## 7. Troubleshooting
I12 uses a wrong environment resource reference. Start with identity and exact name/region, then policies and explicit denies; include relevant KMS and endpoint conditions only when evidence warrants. For missing CloudWatch data distinguish absent ingestion from a wrong dimension/query. Verify with the original operation after an approved fix, plus a forbidden operation that must remain denied.

## 8. Interview preparation
Q23/Q24: tag versus digest and secret rotation versus app refresh. Explain state confidentiality and how a metric alarm can miss a real incident due to scope or evaluation settings.

## 9. Independent practice
Design a release evidence record linking image digest, environment, secret reference (not value) and monitoring tags. Challenge I12 -> H12 -> S12. No actual bucket, registry or secret must be created.

## 10. Revision
Service purpose, identity, network and configuration are separate. Revisit Service routing from day 9 and explain why an API AccessDenied differs from a TCP timeout.

# Day 6: Build one service and Docker image

Resume: R05/R11/R29/R45-R50. Time: 20/40/20/10. Local Docker Desktop; image downloads need internet and disk space. No cloud resources.

## 1. Learning objectives
Build and run one service, explain its entrypoint, and distinguish source, artifact, image and process. Choose Python hands-on today; Java alternatives are in the secondary-tools reference, not extra required builds.

## 2. Concepts
An image is a filesystem/configuration template; a container is an isolated running process using that image. Layers support reuse and caching. Build context is the set of files available to COPY; .dockerignore reduces accidental inclusion. A volume stores data beyond the container's writable layer. EXPOSE documents a port but does not publish it. Multi-stage builds separate compilation from the final runtime; this small standard-library Python example needs no compiler stage.

## 3. How it works
Docker CLI -> daemon -> Dockerfile instructions -> image -> configured process. On macOS Linux containers run inside Docker Desktop's VM. Java normally builds a JAR with Maven or Gradle; Python here runs source with no third-party dependency. USER restricts runtime identity; CMD uses exec form so signals reach Python directly. The process must bind 0.0.0.0 inside the container for published connections.

## 4. Real-world usage
The resume describes CI publishing images to ECR and EKS pulling them. Immutable digests identify bytes; a mutable tag can point elsewhere later. Never bake credentials into ENV, build arguments or COPY layers. Runtime memory must account for the language process, not only its heap setting.

## 5. Hands-on lab
Prerequisites: Docker running, port 8080 free. From the content root:
```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s fixtures/app -v
docker build -t academy:1 fixtures/app
docker run --rm --name academy-app -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 academy:1
```
Keep the last command foreground; in another terminal:
```bash
curl --fail --max-time 3 http://127.0.0.1:8080/health
docker inspect --format '{{.Config.User}} {{.State.Running}}' academy-app
docker logs --tail 10 academy-app
docker image inspect --format '{{.Id}}' academy:1
```
Tests check behavior; build creates an image; run publishes only loopback; inspect reads selected fields instead of dumping environment; logs show request evidence. Cleanup: Ctrl+C the foreground container (`--rm` removes it). Keep the image for kind. Do not use global prune commands.

## 6. Expected output
Three passing tests, a built image ID, HTTP health JSON, and `10001:10001 true` while the container runs. Logs contain JSON request status/duration. A local image ID is not necessarily a registry manifest digest; record the appropriate identity when later publishing.

## 7. Troubleshooting
I06: distinguish build failure, startup exit, wrong bind address and wrong publication. Check first failing layer, CMD, selected state and logs. A missing image in kind is not fixed by rebuilding in the host daemon alone; load it in day 8. Verify a response after the smallest fix.

## 8. Interview preparation
Q11/Q12: explain image/container, build versus runtime, non-root, cache and multi-stage purpose. Use the actual lab as evidence; do not claim you built all resume services independently.

## 9. Independent practice
Build a second image tag from a working copy, change only APP_VERSION at runtime and verify it on `/`. Explain what changed in image identity versus container configuration. Challenge I06 -> H06 -> S06 after a recorded attempt.

## 10. Revision
EXPOSE is not publish; localhost inside a container is not the Mac; tags and digests differ. Save the verified command and selected evidence, not full inspect output or secrets.

# Day 10: EKS-specific architecture and failures

Resume: R02-R04/R19/R23; C03/C10. Time: 20/40/20/10. Local observations plus synthetic EKS evidence; no AWS provisioning.

## 1. Learning objectives
Identify AWS-managed and customer-managed responsibilities. Separate node readiness, Pod networking, DNS, authentication and authorization failures.

## 2. Concepts
EKS manages the Kubernetes control plane. You still manage version decisions, workloads, permissions, add-ons and node capacity/configuration according to the chosen compute mode. EC2-backed managed node groups supply workers; EKS support does not mean you personally provisioned them. VPC CNI allocates networking addresses; CoreDNS resolves names; kube-proxy handles Service rules in common configurations. Managed does not mean maintenance-free.

## 3. How it works
An authenticated client reaches the EKS API, then Kubernetes authorization decides allowed actions. Access entries or legacy mappings depend on cluster configuration. A Pod's AWS identity is separate from the human's cluster access; compare IRSA and EKS Pod Identity without claiming either was used at work. Node registration, runtime health, network setup and DNS have distinct evidence sources.

## 4. Real-world usage
The resume claims one cluster per account/environment. Failure isolation and identity boundaries are important follow-ups. A namespace cannot replace account-level policies. An IP-exhausted subnet can block new Pods despite available CPU; scaling nodes may worsen address pressure.

## 5. Hands-on lab
Inspect analogous local components, then study I10:
```bash
kubectl --context kind-academy get nodes -o wide
kubectl --context kind-academy -n kube-system get deployments,daemonsets
kubectl --context kind-academy -n kube-system logs deployment/coredns --tail=20
ruby -rjson -e 'puts JSON.pretty_generate(JSON.parse(File.read("content/troubleshooting/incidents.json")).find { |item| item["id"] == "I10" })'
```
List what exists locally and what does not: kind does not have AWS VPC CNI simply because it has Pods. Build a node -> CNI -> DNS -> workload checklist from the evidence cards. Cleanup: none.

## 6. Expected output
Local nodes and CoreDNS plus a fixture containing `FailedCreatePodSandBox` and AWS CNI address-allocation evidence. A CoreDNS log can be quiet without being broken. The expected deliverable is a reasoned failure boundary and targeted next check, not a successful EKS deployment claim.

## 7. Troubleshooting
I10: Node NotReady suggests conditions/kubelet/runtime; sandbox creation suggests CNI; name failure with working IP suggests DNS. In an approved nonproduction EKS cluster, read aws-node logs and subnet free-address metadata only with explicit context/account checks. Propose verified capacity/address remediation, not blind restart of all system Pods. Retest scheduling, DNS and application path separately.

## 8. Interview preparation
Q19/Q20: explain control-plane responsibility and why spare CPU does not prove schedulability. Discuss identity permission failures separately from network timeouts.

## 9. Independent practice
Draw EKS API access, Pod AWS API access and user-to-app traffic as three paths. Label actors and permissions. Challenge I10 -> H10 -> S10. Optional approved EKS commands and costs are in Project 2; no paid resources are required today.

## 10. Revision
Do not equate kind with EKS. Record uncertainties about the resume's actual node type, add-ons and auth mode. Revisit IAM's actor/action/resource model.

# Day 13: GitHub Actions, build/test and Snyk

Resume: R27-R29/R39/R44-R50; C07-C09/C20. Time: 20/40/20/10. Local workflow study; hosted execution is optional and may consume Actions minutes.

## 1. Learning objectives
Explain event -> workflow -> job -> runner -> step. Diagnose the earliest causal failure and distinguish build/test/scan/publish responsibilities.

## 2. Concepts
Git records commits; branches name lines of work; a PR proposes reviewable changes. A workflow is YAML automation triggered by events. Jobs run on runners; steps share that job's workspace. Artifacts retain outputs; caches speed reproducible dependency retrieval but are not release evidence. Secrets are protected inputs, not safe to echo. Snyk checks dependency or image findings; policy decides what blocks release.

## 3. How it works
Event/filter -> job permissions/environment -> checkout -> runtime setup -> tests -> build -> artifact. Steps normally stop after failure; careless `continue-on-error` or a swallowed exit status can bypass a gate. Java compiles/packages via Maven/Gradle; Python needs its own dependencies/test runner. Our sample uses unittest, not an invented production Python toolchain.

## 4. Real-world usage
The resume describes standardized workflows and debugging builds across environments. Reuse shared logic with explicit inputs and approvals; do not inject production access into pull-request jobs. Slack notification delivery is separate from build success.

## 5. Hands-on lab
Read `fixtures/github-actions/checks.yml` and annotate every field. It is intentionally outside `.github/workflows` so it cannot execute here. Run its local steps:
```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s fixtures/app -v
docker build -t academy:checks fixtures/app
git --version
```
Tests are the behavior gate; build creates a local image only. For a separate, explicitly authorized training repository containing this content at its root, the workflow can later be copied to `.github/workflows/checks.yml`; do not push during content study. Review the Snyk sample findings in the secondary-tools reference, distinguish app package versus base image, and write a remediation decision. Cleanup: retain the known local image or remove only `academy:checks` after verifying it is unused.

For the C09 standardization exercise, compare `reusable-checks.yml`, `dev-caller.yml` and `qa-caller.yml` in the same fixture directory. Both callers invoke one job-level reusable workflow; a required string input is validated against dev/qa through an environment variable rather than interpolated into shell code. These files remain inactive here. A later authorized repo would need all three in `.github/workflows`; the local `uses` reference resolves there, not in this fixture directory. This example shares validation only, not a deployment or production secret. Independently propose a compatible interface change and show how both callers would be checked.

## 6. Expected output
Passing unittest output and a built image. A failing test must stop publishing. Local YAML parsing cannot prove hosted events, credentials, permissions or minutes are configured correctly; those remain untested until authorized execution.

## 7. Troubleshooting
I13: first ask whether a run exists. If not, inspect event/branch/path filters and workflow location; if queued, inspect runner availability; if failed, identify the first failing step and causal log. Reproduce the same runtime/command locally where possible. Fix only that stage and rerun its test before the whole pipeline. Never log all environment variables for diagnosis.

## 8. Interview preparation
Q25/Q26: artifact versus cache, job versus step, test failure versus compiler failure. A strong answer identifies the failure signal and explains how verification prevents a false-green release.

## 9. Independent practice
Write a workflow requiring tests before image build, with read-only repository permission and no AWS credentials. Explain how you would share it across two environments without duplicating all logic. Challenge I13 -> H13 -> S13 after an attempt.

## 10. Revision
Trigger, runner, command, status and evidence are separate. Revisit Bash exit propagation. Snyk findings are inputs to a remediation process, not proof that all vulnerabilities are exploitable or fixed.

# Day 14: OIDC, ECR and secure publishing

Resume: R03/R05/R28/R29/R43/R44; C07/C19/C20. Time: 20/40/20/10. Core policy/log simulation; real ECR publishing is optional, approved and chargeable.

## 1. Learning objectives
Explain temporary AWS credentials, restricted trust, repository permissions and image identity. Separate authentication failure from denied ECR access.

## 2. Concepts
OIDC is signed identity assertion. GitHub issues a token with audience (`aud`) and subject (`sub`) describing the workload context. STS exchanges an accepted token for temporary role credentials. `id-token: write` permits requesting a GitHub token; it does not grant AWS API permissions. A job using environment `lab` has a different subject from a branch-only job.

## 3. How it works
Approved job -> token -> IAM trust evaluation -> STS credentials -> ECR login -> build/push -> digest -> reviewed deployment-config change. Trust and repository permissions are separate policies. An environment-subject trust policy should be paired with GitHub environment branch restrictions and required reviewers; the subject alone does not constrain the branch.

## 4. Real-world usage
The resume explicitly says **supported** OIDC. Explain your actual contribution without claiming sole architecture ownership. CI should not need permanent AWS keys. A successfully pushed image does not automatically change Helm or ArgoCD desired state.

## 5. Hands-on lab
```bash
python3 -m json.tool fixtures/aws/oidc-trust.json
python3 -m json.tool fixtures/aws/ecr-publish-policy.json
ruby -rjson -e 'puts JSON.pretty_generate(JSON.parse(File.read("content/troubleshooting/incidents.json")).find { |item| item["id"] == "I14" })'
```
Compare synthetic token aud/sub with trust conditions. Inspect the inactive `publish.yml`: manual approval boolean, main guard, lab environment, narrow permissions, account check, credential action, password-stdin login and source-SHA tag. Identify every REPLACE/000000000000 placeholder. Do not copy a company role ARN. Project 3 contains the approved-account procedure; today's task stops at policy reasoning. Cleanup: none.

Alternative 40-minute local publishing block after day 6: verify Docker is ready, port 5001 and container name academy-registry are unused, and keep the registry loopback-only. Downloading the registry image consumes setup time and requires internet:
```bash
docker run -d --rm --name academy-registry -p 127.0.0.1:5001:5000 registry:2.8.3
docker tag academy:1 localhost:5001/academy:1
docker push localhost:5001/academy:1
curl --fail --max-time 3 http://127.0.0.1:5001/v2/academy/tags/list
docker pull localhost:5001/academy:1
```
The tag chooses a registry/repository/tag; push uploads content and reports a digest; the HTTP request lists stored tags; pull verifies registry retrieval. Record the reported digest, not a fabricated value. This disposable unauthenticated HTTP registry is for loopback teaching only and demonstrates neither AWS identity nor OIDC. Never expose it publicly or globally weaken Docker TLS settings if your installation rejects it. Cleanup only the lab registry with `docker stop academy-registry`; its unmounted registry storage is disposable. The original academy:1 image remains for later lessons. Do not run both this block and the full policy exercise as hidden extra homework.

## 6. Expected output
Valid dummy JSON and an evidence-backed mismatch diagnosis. Syntax success does not prove a trusted provider exists. For a later approved push, success means a registry manifest/digest is retrievable, not simply that `docker login` succeeded.

## 7. Troubleshooting
I14: check job token permission, expected aud/sub, correct provider/role and trust restrictions before repository permissions. If STS works but push fails, inspect ECR region, repository, authorization token and upload actions. Do not fix trust with `repo:*`. Verify the intended job succeeds and an unintended repo/environment cannot assume the role.

## 8. Interview preparation
Q27/Q28: explain all authentication steps and why credentials still exist temporarily. Describe how to pin reviewed action SHAs and protect the job environment in a real deployment; the examples use readable version tags for teaching, not a production supply-chain guarantee.

## 9. Independent practice
Draft trust for one fictional repository/environment and a separate ECR publish policy. Predict how the subject changes when you remove `environment: lab`. Challenge I14 -> H14 -> S14 after your attempt.

## 10. Revision
Trust decides who assumes; role policy decides what they do. Never print tokens or run an authenticated curl with verbose headers into evidence. Revisit HPA prerequisites as a separate permission/metrics boundary.

# Day 19: Helm chart fundamentals

Resume: R13/R16/R17/R31/R32; C11. Time: 20/40/20/10. Local rendering requires Helm only; deployment uses the named kind cluster.

## 1. Learning objectives
Explain how chart metadata, templates and values become Kubernetes resources. Inspect rendered output before applying it.

## 2. Concepts
A chart packages templates/defaults/metadata. Chart.yaml describes chart name/version/type; appVersion describes the app but does not automatically change the image. Values configure templates. Helpers share naming logic. A release is an installed Helm instance; chart version, release revision and image version are different identifiers. Quotes matter when a value such as an image tag must remain a string.

## 3. How it works
Load defaults -> merge supplied values -> validate schema -> evaluate templates/functions -> produce YAML -> Kubernetes validates/applies when installing. `include` calls a helper; `toYaml` serializes objects; `nindent` manages indentation. A render can be syntactically valid but point at the wrong port/image or lack a required API.

## 4. Real-world usage
The resume's chart-authoring claim requires understanding the templates, not only running helm upgrade. Reuse should preserve meaningful differences between services. Do not template real credentials into a chart or commit rendered Secrets.

## 5. Hands-on lab
Read every file in `fixtures/helm/academy` and render locally:
```bash
helm lint fixtures/helm/academy
helm template academy fixtures/helm/academy --namespace academy-helm
helm template academy fixtures/helm/academy --set-string image.tag=2
```
Lint checks common chart problems; template renders without cluster contact; set-string overrides just the image tag. Trace the helper-generated name `academy-academy`, Service selector and Pod label. Compare output to the day 8 workload. Optional install alternative after loading image academy:1 into kind:
```bash
helm upgrade --install academy fixtures/helm/academy --kube-context kind-academy --namespace academy-helm --create-namespace --wait --timeout 90s
kubectl --context kind-academy -n academy-helm get deployments,services
```
This separate namespace avoids ownership conflicts with day 8's manually managed resources. Cleanup when finished with Helm lessons: `helm uninstall academy --kube-context kind-academy -n academy-helm`; retain it until day 20 if continuing.

## 6. Expected output
Lint passes; render includes a Deployment and Service with matching selectors, port 80 -> named http/8080 and ready/health probes. A tag override changes image reference, not appVersion metadata. Installation must also prove rollout/readiness; rendering alone does not.

## 7. Troubleshooting
I19: distinguish template parsing, schema validation, YAML structure, API rejection and runtime failure. Inspect the first error and affected rendered field. Correct the smallest type/indent/value issue and rerender before any cluster retry. Use `--debug` only with non-secret lab values; it can expose content.

## 8. Interview preparation
Q37/Q38: chart versus release versus app version; how helper scope, quoting and values affect output. Explain why successful lint is necessary but insufficient.

## 9. Independent practice
Add a non-secret environment setting in a working copy, with a default and a verified rendered change. Write a helper yourself. Challenge I19 -> H19 -> S19 after an attempt; do not copy the guided template as your independent artifact.

## 10. Revision
Values are inputs, manifests are output, cluster state is observation. Revisit Terraform module contracts and avoid treating reuse as hidden configuration magic.

# Day 20: Helm environments and release safety

Resume: R20-R22/R31/R32/R56; C11/C13/C21. Time: 20/40/20/10. Local rendering or one local release exercise, not both plus every optional feature.

## 1. Learning objectives
Compare environment values, validate their types and explain release recovery. Understand HPA/PDB templates without confusing them with installed metrics infrastructure.

## 2. Concepts
Later values files override earlier values; explicit set flags take high precedence. Lists generally replace rather than merge element-by-element, and template behavior still matters. Conditionals include optional resources; range loops render repeated values; helpers keep naming consistent. Dependencies declare charts and need reviewed versions/lockfiles. Upgrade changes a release; rollback restores a previous Helm revision, not external data.

## 3. How it works
Base values + QA override -> schema check -> rendered replica/PDB changes -> API update -> rollout -> readiness. When HPA owns scaling, continuously setting replicas from a chart can conflict with it, so the example omits replicas when autoscaling is enabled. PDB cannot guarantee survival of all node failures.

## 4. Real-world usage
Five environment-specific values files do not mean five unrelated charts. The resume's standardization claim should explain what is shared and how a change is tested before wide adoption. Manual Helm release history differs from ArgoCD using Helm as a renderer.

## 5. Hands-on lab
```bash
helm lint fixtures/helm/academy -f fixtures/helm/qa-values.yaml
helm template academy fixtures/helm/academy -f fixtures/helm/qa-values.yaml
helm template academy fixtures/helm/academy --set autoscaling.enabled=true
helm template academy fixtures/helm/academy --set-string replicaCount=two
```
The first renders QA with two replicas/PDB; the second variant renders HPA; the last intentionally fails the supplied schema and must not be deployed. If doing the installed release option instead, run `helm history academy --kube-context kind-academy -n academy-helm`, upgrade with QA values and verify the Deployment. Only after identifying a known-good prior revision use `helm rollback academy VERIFIED_REVISION --kube-context kind-academy -n academy-helm --wait`; replace that placeholder from actual history. Cleanup: uninstall the named training release after recording evidence.

## 6. Expected output
QA renders two replicas and PDB; autoscaling render includes HPA but no Deployment replicas field. `replicaCount=two` is rejected as a type error. An absent metrics API means HPA cannot obtain useful CPU metrics even though its YAML rendered successfully.

## 7. Troubleshooting
I20: a release timeout can come from probes/image/scheduling, not just Helm syntax. Inspect release status and Kubernetes events/logs, distinguish desired values from running state, and verify recovery with HTTP. Avoid blindly reusing old values that preserve obsolete settings. Prevention: environment render diffs, schema checks and staged validation.

## 8. Interview preparation
Q39/Q40: precedence and rollback limits. Explain what happens when two controllers manage the same field and why GitOps recovery differs from a local Helm rollback.

## 9. Independent practice
Add a typed optional setting and a small range-rendered non-secret environment map in a copy. Define acceptance tests for enabled/disabled cases. Challenge I20 -> H20 -> S20.

## 10. Revision
Validate all target environments, not just defaults. Never call a render a successful deployment. Revisit state locking: tools need clear ownership of desired state.
